newsitem.title: USA: Burlington Northern income falls on bad weather.
newsitem.headline: Burlington Northern income falls on bad weather.

text.p: Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corp. said Tuesday its profits fell 20 percent in the first quarter as bad weather upset its operations and damaged equipment, leading to costly and time-consuming repairs.
Net income for the quarter ended March 31 fell to $150 million, or 95 cents a share, from $187 million or $1.21 per share for the same 1996 period.
The earnings per share were below Wall Street analysts' consensus estimates of 98 cents, according to First Call, which tracks analysts' estimates.
The company said that, while revenues edged up to $2.04 billion from $2.03 billion, operating income slid to $329 million from $385 million.
"Severe weather conditions have affected operations throughout the Northern Plains and the Pacific Northwest since the beginning of the year," Chairman Robert Krebs said in a statement.

"The financial impact of recurring and protracted outages on many parts of the system, the cost of repairing track, signals and equipment, and the operating inefficiencies caused by the weather are virtually impossible to measure," he added.
Burlington Northern estimated that bad weather reduced revenues in the quarter by about $100 million and increased expenses by about $50 million.

"Some carryover effect will be felt in the second quarter because of an April blizzard in the Powder River Basin, which shut down coal operations for two days, and by flooding in the upper Midwest," Krebs said.

Revenues from shipping containers rose 7 percent to $527 million from $491 million, led by increases in direct, international and truckload sectors. Coal revenues of $489 million increased $11 million, or 2 percent.

These increases more than offset a $48 million, or 14 percent, decline in agricultural commodities revenues due mainly to weather-related service problems affecting shipments of wheat, corn and soybeans and a poor winter wheat crop.
Equipment rental costs rose $22 million because of the adverse weather. Fuel expense grew by $28 million due to an 11 cent, or 17 percent, increase in fuel prices.
However, material and other expenses fell to $200 million from $218 million in 1996, when the Fort Worth, Texas-based company had several major derailments.

BNSF, parent company of the Burlington Northern and Santa Fe Railway Co., operates one of the nation's largest railroad networks, with 35,000 route miles of track covering 29 states and two Canadian provinces.
Burlington Northern's stock rose 12.5 cents to $71 early on the New York Stock Exchange.
